description: Composite two-panel figure relating to strengthening of Fe-Mn-Al-C austenite steels. (a) is a line chart of "Yield strength increment, MPa" (vertical axis, -40 to 200, labelled every 40 MPa) versus "Element content, wt.%" (horizontal axis, 0-14, ticks at 2, 4, 6, 8, 10, 12, 14); seven straight lines radiate from the origin, labelled N, C, Mo, V, Si, Mn and Ni, with the C and Mn lines drawn in red; no numeric data labels are printed. (b) plots four "Engineering stress, MPa" versus "Engineering strain, %" curves (stress axis 0 to above 1400 MPa in 200 MPa steps; strain axis 0-60 % in 10 % steps), annotated in-plot with austenite grain sizes d ≈ 1.12 µm, d ≈ 1.48 µm, d ≈ 1.75 µm and d ≈ 20.70 µm. In (a) N is steepest (it crosses the 200 MPa gridline before 2 wt%), the red C line is next (about 150 MPa at 2 wt%), followed by Mo, V and Si, while red Mn stays almost flat and Ni lies slightly below zero. In (b) the finest grain size (1.12 µm) shows the highest plateau stress and shortest elongation (~42 % strain), the 20.70 µm sample the lowest plateau (~800 MPa) but longest elongation (~57 %). The figure links solid-solution hardening coefficients (a) to grain-refinement (Hall-Petch) strengthening (b).

subfigures.description: Line chart: yield strength increment (MPa, -40 to 200, 40 MPa gridlines) vs element content (wt.%, 0-14). Seven straight lines from the origin labelled N, C, Mo, V, Si, Mn, Ni; C and Mn lines coloured red. N is steepest and crosses the 200 MPa gridline below 2 wt%; C (red) ends near 150 MPa at 2 wt%; Mo, V and Si are progressively shallower; Mn (red) is nearly horizontal and Ni lies slightly below zero. No data labels printed.

Engineering stress-strain curves (stress 0 to >1400 MPa, strain 0-60 %) for four austenite grain sizes, labelled in-plot: d ≈ 1.12 µm (highest plateau, ends near 42 % strain), d ≈ 1.48 µm (ends near 52 %), d ≈ 1.75 µm (ends near 48 %), d ≈ 20.70 µm (lowest plateau, about 800 MPa, elongation near 57 %).

observations.observation: Panel (a) axes are labelled 'Yield strength increment, MPa' (-40 to 200) versus 'Element content, wt.%' (0 to 14, ticks every 2).
Panel (a) contains seven straight lines issuing from the origin, labelled N, C, Mo, V, Si, Mn and Ni; the C and Mn lines are printed in red, the others black.
In panel (a) the N line has the steepest slope, crossing the 200 MPa gridline below 2 wt% content, and the red C line is the next steepest, ending near 150 MPa at about 2 wt%.
In panel (a) the Mo, V and Si lines are progressively shallower (Mo ends near the 110 MPa line at about 6 wt%, V near 70 MPa at about 9 wt%, Si near 50 MPa at about 10 wt%).

In panel (a) the red Mn line is almost horizontal, rising only to roughly the 10-15 MPa level at 14 wt%, whereas the Ni line lies below the zero line (about -20 MPa at ~7 wt%), i.e. Ni gives a slightly negative yield-strength increment.
No numeric data labels or values are printed on either panel; values can only be read against the gridlines.
Panel (b) axes are labelled 'Engineering stress, MPa' (0 to above 1400, ticks every 200) and 'Engineering strain, %' (0 to 60, ticks every 10).
Panel (b) shows four engineering stress-strain curves annotated in-plot with d ≈ 1.12 µm, d ≈ 1.48 µm, d ≈ 1.75 µm and d ≈ 20.70 µm.

In panel (b) the curve for d ≈ 1.12 µm has the highest plateau stress and the shortest elongation (~42 % strain), while the curve for d ≈ 20.70 µm has the lowest plateau (~800 MPa) and the longest elongation (~57 %).

The caption states that (a) shows the contributed yield strength increment of alloying elements in austenite steel [6] and (b) engineering stress-strain curves of samples with various austenite grain sizes [48].
The citing text states that 1 wt% C contributes 187-300 MPa to the yield strength of austenite and that 1 wt% Al contributes slightly below 10 MPa; no Al line is plotted in panel (a).

The citing text states that interstitial C and N atoms in FCC γ-Fe cause lattice distortion and strong hardening, whereas substitutional atoms such as Mn, Ni or Si produce spherically symmetric distortion and weaker strengthening, which is the ordering seen in panel (a) (N and C steepest, Mn/Ni shallow or negative).

The citing text states that austenite grain refinement raised the yield strength and ultimate tensile strength by more than 400 MPa (Fig. 5b) but that excessively small grains weaken this strengthening effect.

measured_quantities: yield strength increment (MPa) per wt.% element
